## What the model says

The diffusion decision model (DDM; [Ratcliff, 1978](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.85.2.59);
[Ratcliff & McKoon, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.2008.12-06-420)) describes a two-choice decision
as the accumulation of noisy evidence. Evidence starts at `zr` × `bound`, moves on average at rate
`drift` with noise of standard deviation 1 per second, and the decision is made when it first reaches the
upper boundary at `bound` (response 1) or the lower boundary at 0 (response 0). The response time adds
the non-decision time `ndt`, for encoding the stimulus and executing the response. `drift` is the
quality of the evidence; a positive drift favours the upper response, a negative one the lower. `bound` is how much evidence the
participant waits for, and `zr` is a bias toward one response before any evidence arrives.

For a response at the lower boundary at decision time $t$ = rt − `ndt`, with $v$ = `drift`, $a$ = `bound` and
$z_r$ = `zr`, the density is

$$
f_0(t) = \frac{\pi}{a^2}\, e^{-v a z_r - v^2 t / 2} \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k\, e^{-k^2 \pi^2 t / (2 a^2)} \sin(k \pi z_r),
$$

and $f_1(t)$, the density at the upper boundary, is the same with $v$ replaced by $-v$ and $z_r$ by
$1 - z_r$: the same process seen upside down. Each of the two is a defective density: its area is the probability of that response, and
the two areas sum to 1. The noise per unit time, `s`, is fixed at 1 in bmm; it sets the scale on which
the other parameters are measured.

## The task

One trial is a choice between two responses, with the response time recorded: a brightness or a
lexical decision, for example. bmm codes the responses 0 (lower) and 1 (upper); which response is
which is the analyst's choice, often correct as 1 and error as 0. The task panel draws five evidence
paths from the same start under the current parameters, with the noise of each path held fixed while
the sliders move. Paths that end at the upper boundary are blue, those that end at the lower boundary
orange. The grey band is the non-decision time, the dashed line is the mean path, the start plus
`drift` × time, and the bracket on the right marks `bound`. The paths illustrate the process; they are
not data.

## Explore

The density panel shows the two defective densities, upper responses above the axis and lower
responses below. Raising `drift` moves area from the lower to the upper density. Moving it away from 0,
in either direction, makes both faster: the response-time distribution of each response depends on the
size of `drift`, not on its sign.
Raising `bound` makes both slower and more spread out and, for a drift other than 0, moves area toward
the response the drift favours. `ndt` shifts both densities without changing their shape. Moving `zr`
toward 1 makes upper responses more frequent and faster and lower responses rarer and slower.
P(upper), the probability of response 1, and the mean response times in the readout come from exact
formulas for this process, the same ones the [EZ diffusion page](ezdm.qmd) uses.

Slider ranges come from bmm's default priors for `ddm()`. `bound` is estimated on the log scale with a
normal(0, 0.5) prior, `ndt` on the log scale with normal(−1.5, 0.5), and `zr` on the logit scale with
normal(0, 0.5); each slider spans the prior mean ± 3 SD: `bound` from 0.22 to 4.48, `ndt` from 0.05
to 1 s, `zr` from 0.18 to 0.82. `drift` has an identity link and a cauchy(0, 1) prior, which has no
standard deviation; its slider spans the location ± 3 scale, from −3 to 3. The sliders start at the
prior means (dashed): `drift` = 0, `bound` = 1, `ndt` = 0.22 s, `zr` = 0.5. With no drift and the start
in the middle, both responses are equally likely.

## Across task settings

The likelihood of `ddm()` has no task-setting variable. Conditions of an experiment, for example easy
and hard stimuli or instructions to be fast or accurate, enter only if the bmm formula lets the
parameters differ between them, as in `drift ~ 0 + difficulty`. What the model then predicts in each
condition follows from the estimated parameters.

Speed and accuracy are both outcomes of the same parameters, and the panel *Speed and accuracy as bound
changes* shows how they trade. As `bound` grows from 0.22 to 4.48 with the other parameters fixed, the mean response time grows,
and P(upper) moves toward 1 for a positive drift (toward 0 for a negative one). With `drift` at 0
the line is flat: waiting for more evidence costs time and buys no accuracy, because the evidence
favours neither response. bmm's DDM article reads `bound` as response caution, the parameter behind a
speed/accuracy trade-off, and `drift` as the quality of the evidence or the difficulty of the task.

## In bmm

```{=html}
<div class="ex-widget">
  <pre class="ex-code" id="ddm-code"></pre>
  <button type="button" class="btn btn-sm btn-outline-secondary" id="ddm-copy">Copy</button>
</div>
<script type="module" src="../js/pages/ddm.js"></script>
```

The code updates with the controls. `ddm()` defines the model, `dddm()` returns the log density of
response times and responses, and `bmf()` writes the formula for `bmm()`, which estimates the parameters
from trial-level data; `my_data` stands for your own data, and fitting runs Stan through brms. The
comment under the `dddm()` call holds the values this page computes for it. `dddm()` calls
`rtdists::ddiffusion()`, which sums either the series above or a second series that converges faster at
short decision times, whichever needs fewer terms, and stops after enough terms for an absolute error of
about 10⁻⁶ in the density. Where a density is very small, far in a tail, an error of that size is large
against the value, so the cut-off decides it; this page follows the same rule, so it shows what bmm
returns. See the
[DDM article](https://venpopov.com/bmm/articles/bmm_ddm.html) for the full model and the reference pages
for [`ddm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/ddm.html) and
[`dddm()`](https://venpopov.com/bmm/reference/ddm_dist.html).
